[h3]Summary[/h3] The game is really good quality-wise, but I'm no longer the target demographic thus I can't recommend it. [h3]The good[/h3] The game has some really fun gameplay, fantastic scenary (it really feel like a theme-park ride) and breathe high quality in atmosphere, graphics, sound (cars, music and commentator) and it simply feels great to drive. [h3]The Bad[/h3] Starting the game you have to log into your MS-account, connect your accounts and connect to it whenever you start the game (I couldn't find a way to start the game without it). No big deal, but it was 5 minutes of direct annoyance and if my internet goes I can't boot the game. Playing for around 2 hours I got hit by 3 fullscreen splash screens that locked my game until I removed it, straight after a race, in-game, that tried to sell me the new game FH6, missing DLC etc. The in-game store is very noticable with "new notifications"-marks and it's part of the main menu. It felt like a mobile game in that regard. [h3]The Demographic[/h3] The game start with blasting off straight away, you get thrown into epic race scenes for about 5-10 minutes, which feel great, then you hit the character creation screen. It's a loud white and pink colored UI (which is the UI for the rest of the game). The first tab is to choose between very ethnically varied characters, next is genders including they/them... an two large tabs for choosing prosthetics and hearing aids... It's not a bad thing per se, but resources were spent on quite a lot of options that, to me, has no place in a racing game and is clearly catering to a certain crowd. After playing for 2 hours, I realized this was a theme. This game is very much trying to vibe with the "modern audiances" with bright colors and a chirpy attitude. I am not a fan of that. I wanted a simcade with muscle/super cars, high octane racing and a badass feel in a sleek upgraded package. I've realized I'm not the target demographic anymore, which is my issue and not the game being bad. However, it really pulls me out of the immersion. The Steam store pictures and trailers show none of this and all the focus is on cool cars going fast (in hindsight, the opening of the second trailer really hints at it). Thank god for Steam's refund policy.

Elden Ring is one of those games that was elevated to fame even before its release. From Software, creators of the Dark Souls series, the game was billed as an extension of the familiar open-world formula. However, the end result is more complex. It's a game with many great ideas, but also with distinct design issues that often impact gameplay. Character Development System: One of the game's greatest strengths is the sheer variety of builds. Players can develop their characters in many ways, from the classic warrior with heavy weapons, through quick, arcade-based builds, to powerful magic-based characters. The development system offers significant freedom and encourages experimentation. However, the problem arises during gameplay. Quite often, a build that previously worked very well suddenly ceases to be effective. At some point, we hit a wall, and enemies or bosses become significantly more difficult for a given playstyle. As a result, instead of developing a character according to their own vision, the player begins to adapt to the demands of specific battles. Visuals and Game World: From an artistic perspective, the game looks excellent. The world is vast, diverse, and full of distinctive locations, and each region has its own unique atmosphere and visual identity. The world's history, co-created by George R. R. Martin, is also noteworthy. The lore is engaging and intriguing, though much of the plot remains hidden within item descriptions and dialogue fragments. For some, this is a key element in the world's mystery, while for others, it's a barrier to understanding the story. Camera Issues: The game's biggest flaw is the camera. This is where most frustrating situations arise. During combat, you can lock the camera onto a target. In theory, this is supposed to aid in tracking the opponent, but in practice, it often leads to chaos. The camera can get lost, suddenly change position, or be positioned at an awkward angle. As a result, the player cannot see enemy attacks, nor even their own character. The problem is particularly acute with large enemies. The camera can then position itself so close to the boss model that it's difficult to assess the situation on screen. Attempting to play without target lock also doesn't solve the problem, as the camera can still move on its own and doesn't always stay where the player intended it to be. In practice, this means that some deaths aren't due to player error or combat difficulty, but rather to technical and design issues. Repetitive Enemy and Boss Characters: Another drawback is the enemy design and the repetitive nature of many fights. In many places, the copy-and-paste method is evident. A boss, who we previously fought in a spectacular fight, later reappears as a regular enemy in a different location. This weakens the sense of uniqueness of the encounters and makes some moments less impactful. Battles can be spectacular, but that doesn't always mean they're well-designed. Some encounters feel heavily scripted. Sometimes, it feels as if they can only be completed sensibly with one specific playstyle, as other approaches are significantly more challenging. Approaching New Players: The game also disrespects players new to Souls games. At many points, it assumes the player already knows the mechanics characteristic of the genre. The game's systems are poorly explained, and many things have to be discovered through trial and error. The franchise's popularity is largely based on its reputation for exceptional difficulty. In practice, however, a significant portion of this difficulty stems from design issues. Unclear combat, camera issues, and inconsistent design decisions make the game challenging not because the enemies are well-designed, but because certain game elements make it difficult to play comfortably. The spawn point system is a good example of inconsistent design. Sometimes, a bonfire is located directly in front of the boss arena, with a statue allowing you to respawn even closer. In other situations, each death requires a long journey from the bonfire to the boss gate. With more difficult enemies, such as Malenia and the Blade of Miquella, this means that a significant portion of the time isn't devoted to the fight itself. Instead, the player runs back to the arena and reapplies buffs before the fight. As a result, up to a quarter of the time spent on a boss can simply consist of repeating the same path. Summary: Elden Ring is a game full of contrasts. On the one hand, it offers a beautiful world, interesting lore, and vast character building opportunities. On the other hand, it suffers from obvious design issues, such as camera work, repetitive enemies, and inconsistent combat design. It's not a bad game, but it's definitely not as flawless as some reviews suggest. Some players elevate it to a pedestal. This is mainly due to the reputation of the FromSoftware studio, and not necessarily due to the actual quality of all the game's elements. It's a title that manages to delight with its vision of the world, but at the same time, it can also be very frustrating at times.

I have played this game a lot, both with and without mods. I'll be blunt: it's a good game overall, but it has a lot of things dragging it down. Some say it's a 10/10 game, but I disagree. First of all, the biggest issue with this game, is input reading. Enemies and bosses don't react to what you do, they react the moment you press a button, before your action has even started. The enemy in Fort Gael is a good example: I try to shoot it with a crossbow, but it evade the moment I press the button, wether I'm aiming at it or not. This is dumb. -1 point. Next is wind-up attacks and tracking: a lot of bosses and enemies have ridiculous wind-ups that mess up dodge timing and ruins the rythm of the fight. And if you try to reposition to avoid it completely, they will simply turn around 180 degrees and hit you with that attack anyway. This is cheap, not difficoult. -1 point. Then there is the game balance: it feels like they spent less than 10 minuttes to balance this game. In a lot of late game areas, enemies are just basic scrubs that do nothing, while a mid game area might have enemies that will utterly destroy you regardless of stats and defence. Bosses also do WAYYYY too much damage in proportion to how often they attack and how long their combos are. They get to kill me in 2-3 hits while being able to chain 3-7 attacks in a row, while I'm lucky to land 1 single hit before they jump away from me and just stare at me from the other side of the area. This is utterly stupid. -2 points. Next is the ability to respec, upgrade weapons, and change builds: this is hopeless.... the game is incredibly stingy with upgrade materials, and even if you obtain the bellbearings, the mats get increasingly expensive. You need a total of 12 of each basic smithingstone to max a weapon, from lvl 1 stones to lvl 9 stones. And lvl 8 stones cost 30 000 runes a piece, just to give an example. This discourages experimentation in a game with over 100 weapons. Respecing is also limited, as there is a fixed amount of larval tears you can obtain in a single playthrough. This can hardlock you to stick with the same build through the whole game. -2 points. Now we are down to 4/10. Now lets add the good things: The world is big, with lots of things to discover around every corner. Everything from weapons, mats and spells, to catacombs, castles and dungeons. Exploration is very rewarding. +2 points. Buildvariaty: if we look away from the horrible upgrade system, there is a lot of different ways to build your character. You can go pure meele, or pure spell/incantation builds, or heavily focus on status buildup, or make a combination of either of them, and much more. +1 point. Encounters: there are many npcs to stumble upon in this game, most of wich leads to new side quests or detours, or even new areas. Some are missable, wich can lead to missing out on certain questlines or items, but this isn't really a problem. The npcs of this game are fairly interesting, and some will even fight alongside you at certain bosses if you summon them. +1 point. Now we are at 8/10. There is a lot more that drag this game both up and down, but these are my takes. Personally I give the game a 7/10. It's an overall good game, especially with certain mods, but it can be really frustrating at times, and I can't really think of anyone I would ever recommend this game to. I had my fun, along with much frustration. Edit: Steam doesn't ask if the game is good, Steam ask if I would recommend it. I would not, unless it is with mods.

God I could write a novel on my mixed feelings on this one - approaching 6 years of 2077 here, good lorde. Few games had me as hyped as Cyberpunk 2077. From its 2015 reveal to the delayed 2020 launch, I was completely locked in, in 2015 I basically discovered the cyberpunk genre through the world Mike Pondsmith created. It felt like the perfect middle ground between overdone fantasy and surface-level sci-fi. This was the only game I have ever preordered. I played it at launch on PC and, despite bugs like T-posing, broken AI, and weird visual glitches, I still enjoyed my first run. A lot of the bigger issues felt fixable, and I was more excited for what the game could become. Things like deeper RPG systems, meaningful AI, gang dynamics, and customization all felt like they were coming later. That is where the disappointment really sets in. Even now in 2026, after patches and Cyberpunk 2077: Phantom Liberty, it never became the RPG it was presented as. If you were (like me) expecting something closer to The Witcher but in a cyberpunk setting, this is not that. And yet I have played through it six+ times. Because what is here is still incredible. Night City is one of the most detailed and immersive worlds ever made. Just driving around, watching the skyline, and existing in that space is unmatched. It honestly feels like the scale and ambition of the world came at the cost of the systems meant to support it. Amazing world, unforgettable vibe, but a missed RPG opportunity, and they clearly knew it from how they focused on all its positives in Phantom Liberty.

Never goes super in depth with its mechanics or balances them well. Not even the start feels that balanced. But it does enough with what it has to keep you playing. It definitely does tickle your bone in your body that likes to explore from time to time (lest you'll probably have to wiki-dive for questions you have). The highlight of the game isn't really the farming. Everything related to crops or animals isn't that rewarding besides easy money. There's maybe a few days of unique content that you'll likely care about, everything else is intermittent. The other skills will probably interest you more if you want more active gameplay. Many say to not do a modded playthrough the first time but I would say honestly give it a shot if the game doesn't interest you in some aspects. I've had way much more fun with faster animations + marriage mod (the marriage candidate pool is limited and the gameplay loop is a bit slow, especially when trying to go through all its content). I probably would've had even more fun with something like SDVE (Stardew Valley Expanded) as it mostly adds on to already existing content. This is a really safe pick if you want to play something low-pressure with your friends so it's also great for that.

10/10 I first played Hades when it was in Early Access, and I really liked what I saw back then, but, for external reasons, I ended up leaving the game behind and never really played it again, even though I'd seen the game getting massively positive reviews everywhere (well, of course, the game really IS everything people say it is). This year, I decided to return to Hades with getting 100% completion in mind, since I really wanted to play Hades II, and I wouldn't play it without completing everything in Hades first, so my journey began; The thing is, there is nothing special about my ¡°journey¡± playing Hades, nothing too different from the majority of players' experiences, but the ¡°conventional¡± experience was already enough to make it a blast. I've played a lot of roguelikes in my life (and still do, by the way; it's by far my favorite genre out there), and Hades is easily tied for first place with The Binding of Isaac. I'm not really trying to compare them, but I genuinely can't say one is better than the other, since both are 10/10 in their own ways. The game is just too good. The story itself is phenomenal, and the way it blends with the roguelike genre is also just chef's kiss. There isn't a single character that I didn't end up liking lol. The gameplay itself is also on another level. In my first ten hours I thought the weapons and boons weren't that many but after 70 hours, I can confidently say: there really are that many. It's not that there are a lot of weapons or a massive amount of boons (power-ups) to choose from, but they blend so well with each other and make the gameplay feel so different from before that it's completely worth it. Also, about the story, there's something really cool: the game could technically end earlier if you don't want to spend that much time on it (though I honestly don't know why you wouldn't). The game basically has ¡°two endings¡±; the first one starts the credits scene and you could say that's the end of the story if you want, but after that there is the ¡°post-credits¡± section where you can keep playing and the story basically keeps moving forward, more than doubling your playtime. The thing is, if you want to stop there or take a break from the game, you won't really be missing much, at least not nearly as much as if you stopped before the climax, I mean. As someone who deeply loves the roguelike genre, I feel SO happy that Hades exists. As I've said before, to me, Hades is just on another level compared to most other games in the genre. The story is fantastic. The gameplay is some of the most addictive and enjoyable out there. The voice acting and performances of all the characters are more than just on point: it's honestly absurd how good they are. And I WON'T even start talking about the OST, or else I'll never stop (It's also chef's kiss, who would've thought?) Truly a masterpiece. - a fellow Dusa fan

One Ring made by the evil lord Sauron Hidetaka Miyazaki, One Ring to rule them all, One Ring to find them, One Ring to bring them all and in the darkness bind them, In the Land of Japanese software development warehouse building where Shadows lie. Elden Ring is not worth your time due to the profound curse placed upon the game's core design by the evil man who made it. The game aims at being infinitely replayable, but each of its assets is designed in a narrow fashion - so much so that the world does not feel as open as it is rather episodic. Each and every instance in the game is instrumented to be seen and encountered in a specific way which makes the experience of world exploration predictable and less exciting after playing for the first time. The dificulty ranges of the various explorable regions of the game world are awfully imballanced, so much so that it's less enjoyable to avoid choosing a linear path through the game on later playthroughs. The game world's incredibly size makes this issue even more frustrating - in order to experience something new on a subsequent playthrough, the player has to cross massive distances which are increasingly less and less aproachable the further he is from the starting point, ultimately discouraging exploration and narrowing the game experience to a single, most optimalized path of progression. There are only so many ways to reexperience the game's world without being severely discouraged and punished. And so ultimately, the game world's size and the quantity of its assets is severely nullified as the various paths to approach them are tragically so very limited. The game's world becomes eventually too predictable and the premise of experiencing the game in a fresh way nonexistent, which is not fun. Let it be pronounced and heard, Elden Ring could be legendary, but it is not, and won't be, unless FromSoftware developpers cease to practice the habit of forgetting a game once it's been created, despite the quantity of bothersome features still present and still widely acknowledged. One may recall the pathos of never properly finishing Lost Izalith in their previous game Dark Souls, an area of the game so very unique and all the more so disappointing for being critically underdevelopped. I feel very simillar about Elden Ring. As a former world of warcraft player, I see fit to pronounce a variety of ideas which could severely improve the experience of Elden Ring if they were ever developped, as they are present in that particular game, and although a very different game at that, still possesing a massive world and the spirit of an rpg game. Those ideas would be: There should be a variety of start points in Elden Ring, or at the very least, it should be possible to cross into other regions of the game from Limgrave without being stupefied and severely punished as much as is the case now. There should be more low level regions surrounding Limgrave so as to increase replayability and the possibilities of exploration on future playthroughs. And yes, despite the existence of various teleportation chests in Limgrave, the fact that the places you are sent to are completely above Limgrave's difficulty makes them less relevant as a travel feature. There is not enough enemy variety at each of the game's various places - an occasional "rare enemy spawn" or the promise of a "rare item drop" would be a solution to this issue. And lastly, there should be more paths connecting the various regions and places of the Elden Ring world and more accessible ways to connect the game's many features. In conclusion, Elden Ring nowhere near as fun as enjoyable after the first couple of playthroughs, it becomes stale and predictable rather too fast, and that is a completely nonsensical feature for a game of such high ambition and such quantity of the game's features.

My review of Elden Ring After 100 hours!!! And after completing the game 100% I can say it’s not just a game — it’s a legendary masterpiece! At the very least, it’s a complete game. A world with this level of beauty, scale, depth, and visual variety — from lush, green natural lands to desert regions and volcanic areas, from snowy realms and dragon-infested worlds to even an underground world. From the moment you enter the game, you realize you’re standing before the greatest game of the century — perhaps even the greatest thing ever created in gaming. The world design is carefully crafted and precise, but nothing surpasses the mastery and precision of the boss fights. Literally, Souls games are the only ones that have perfected boss combat — where you must memorize the boss’s moves, learn their fighting style, and master dodging with the correct timing. And since we mentioned timing, how can we not bring up parrying with shields — a unique and excellent feature in Souls / Souls-like games. The story has a depth that pulls you into deep thought, and the soundtracks transport you to another world, making the experience even more incredible. The variety of weapons — from magic, swords, bows, and spears — along with the diversity of skills (Ashes of War), adds even more richness. By the way, the game isn’t primarily based on magic, yet it contains hundreds of spells — meaning it even surpasses games that are built around magic, like Hogwarts Legacy. I don’t even know how to describe the greatness of the bosses to you. You’ll face some of the greatest bosses in Souls games — I’m talking about General Radahn, the Starscourge, descendant of war, the Red Lion, breaker of kings, shedder of blood. And I’m talking about Malenia, Lady of the Sword, the undefeated Blade of Miquella, the lone flower of the Elden. And not to mention Godfrey, the first Elden Lord, warrior of kings, breaker of thrones, the White Lion, the embodiment of raw power. The game is difficult and gives you nothing easily, but it rewards every effort you put in and every skill you learn. Every step is calculated, every decision carries weight, every moment is full of excitement, and every minute you spend in the game is a unique experience. Elden Ring is the crown of gaming. It doesn’t just deserve Game of the Year — it deserves Game of the Century. They made this masterpiece in just 5 years, which is honestly insane. Even the biggest studios couldn’t pull off something like this in that time. And yeah, I don’t regret spending a single penny on this game. Thanks, FromSoftware.

I've played Elden Ring more times than I can count, first on PS4 when it launched, then again on PS5, and came back once more when Shadow of the Erdtree dropped, and now on PC, every single run, it still finds a way to impress, the gameplay is the foundation everything else sits on, and FromSoftware absolutely nailed it. The level design is masterful, each region has its own identity and mood, and legacy dungeons like Stormveil and Leyndell are some of the most carefully crafted spaces I've ever explored in a game. The cutscenes are genuinely stunning, the art, the lighting, the scale and the Soundtracks ofc. If you want to start a FromSoftware game, Elden Ring is your go-to, It's far more beginner friendly than people make it out to be, yes there are hard parts, but the summon system is there for a reason, struggling with a boss? Call for help, It genuinely makes the experience more accessible without taking anything away from it. And the DLC, At 40€ Shadow of the Erdtree is a steal, the amount of content, new areas, new weapons, and bosses it brings closer to a full sequel than an expansion, If you loved the base game, this is non-negotiable.
